It doesn't take a hacker to lose a big payment. It takes one email with the bank details quietly changed.

Invoice fraud is one of the most common ways businesses lose real money, and it's convincing. The email looks right, the invoice looks right, only the account number is different. By the time anyone notices, the money's gone.

The fix isn't clever tech, it's a habit. When bank details change, confirm it by phone on a number you already hold, never one from the email.

Everyone has a backup. Almost no one has tested it.

A backup you've never restored from is a guess, not a safety net. Plenty of businesses only find out theirs was failing, half-configured or missing the important stuff on the day they actually need it.

Good backup is the boring kind. It runs, it's checked, and it gets test-restored so you know it works before disaster, not after.

Phishing emails used to be easy to spot. Odd spelling, strange logos, a prince with a fortune to share. Not anymore.

Attackers now use AI to write emails that match your tone, your suppliers and your finance process, so the message asking to update the bank details reads exactly like the real thing.

The old advice, look for typos, doesn't cut it. What works now is a simple rule. Verify any request for money or a detail change another way, every time.

Here's one that catches a lot of people out. "Microsoft 365 backs up our data." It doesn't.

Microsoft keeps the service running. Your actual emails, files and Teams messages are your responsibility. Delete something, get hit by ransomware, or lose a mailbox when someone leaves, and once the short retention window passes, it's gone for good.

A proper 365 backup means you can put it all back in minutes, from any point in time.

If you're not sure whether yours is actually backed up, we'll check for you. Drop us a message.

Ask what an hour of downtime costs and most owners guess low. Then they add up the wages, the stalled orders, the calls that don't get answered and the customers who quietly go elsewhere, and the number jumps.

Downtime is rarely one big disaster. It's the drive that fails on a Monday, the server nobody patched, the internet line with no backup.

Most of it is preventable with the right setup and a bit of planning.

One password used everywhere feels convenient. It's also how one breach becomes all of them.

When a site you use gets hacked, those email-and-password combinations end up on lists that attackers try everywhere else. If the same password opens your email, it opens a lot more.

Two things fix most of this. A password manager, so every login is different, and multi-factor authentication, so a stolen password isn't enough on its own.

Here's an uncomfortable one. Right now, anyone can send an email that looks like it came from your business, unless you've locked your domain down.

Without the right settings (SPF, DKIM and DMARC), scammers can put your company name on an email to your own customers and suppliers. It's a common way invoice fraud starts.

The fix is technical but quick, and once it's done it runs in the background.

When someone leaves, the laptop comes back. Their access often doesn't.

Old logins to email, shared files, apps and remote tools have a habit of lingering long after someone's gone. Each one is a door left open, and nobody's watching it.

A proper leavers process closes accounts, reclaims access and moves their data on the day they go, not weeks later when someone remembers.

Most breaches don't start with the firewall failing. They start with someone clicking.

That's not a dig at your team. The emails are convincing, everyone's busy, and it only takes one rushed moment. Technology alone won't fix it, and blaming people won't either.

What helps is a mix. Filtering that stops most of it reaching inboxes, MFA so one slip isn't a disaster, and short, practical training so people know what to look for.

"Remind me later" isn't a security policy, but for a lot of businesses it's what they've got.

Those update prompts are usually fixing the exact holes attackers are looking for. Put them off for weeks and you're leaving a known door unlocked.

The answer isn't nagging people. It's updates that install quietly in the background, managed centrally, so they just happen without anyone downing tools.

We'll set that up so your team stays current without thinking about it. Drop us a message.

You can lock down your own business and still get caught out through a supplier.

The software you rely on, the bookkeeper with access to your accounts, the vendor plugged into your systems. If their security's weak, that becomes your problem too.

You don't need to audit the world. You do need to know who has access to what, and to ask your key suppliers the basic security questions.
